title: How Trickle-Down Economics Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain trickle-down economics, the idea that cutting taxes or otherwise transferring wealth to the wealthiest will spur investment and job creation that benefits everyone else. They cover the name's origins (Will Rogers in the 1920s, George H. W. Bush's "voodoo economics" jab at Reagan), the contrast between supply-side and Keynesian demand-side thinking, Say's Law and its misinterpretation, Laffer curve and the prohibitive range, examples of Hoover, Harding and Coolidge, Roosevelt, Kennedy and Reagan, Reaganomics debates, Obama's quantitative easing as "trickle-down monetary policy," and a listener's proposal to tax estates at death rather than income. They stress that economics is not a pure science and the effects of these policies are disputed. The episode closes with a listener mail segment from Caleb in Indiana about waiting for dental school results.

segments.title: Opening banter and Ferris Bueller reference
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about trickle names and Chuck's birthday, then bring up Ben Stein's economics teacher role in Ferris Bueller's Day Off and the origin of the term 'voodoo economics' coined by George H. W. Bush.

segments.title: What trickle-down economics means
segments.summary: The hosts define trickle-down economics as placing wealth with the wealthiest so they invest in the economy, creating jobs and wealth that spreads down. They note supply-side advocates dislike the term and that economics is not a pure science.

segments.title: Disputed effects of Reaganomics
segments.summary: The hosts say articles on Reaganomics reach opposite conclusions and that cause and effect is hard to isolate from other factors, such as Clinton-era prosperity and the dot-com boom.

segments.title: Origins of the term and wealth transfer through tax cuts
segments.summary: Will Rogers popularized the phrase in the 1920s. Reagan cut the top tax rate from about 70 percent to about 50 percent. Trickle-down can be done through tax cuts or other means, and it is usually used during slumps.

segments.title: Say's Law and supply versus demand
segments.summary: The hosts explain Jean-Baptiste Say's idea that products are paid for with products, how the popular version 'supply creates its own demand' is a misinterpretation, and how the housing glut illustrates overproduction.

segments.title: Keynesian economics and the policy history
segments.summary: Keynes argued for stimulating demand, not supply. Hoover followed supply-side policy before the Great Depression, and Roosevelt adopted Keynesian policy. Kennedy and then Reagan embraced supply-side ideas.

segments.title: The Laffer curve and the prohibitive range
segments.summary: The Laffer curve describes how tax revenue may fall at very high tax rates because people reduce work. The hosts give a worked example of a 90 percent bracket and describe it as a thought experiment rather than data-based law.

segments.title: How trickle-down works and whether it has worked
segments.summary: Chuck walks through the supply-side mechanism: cut top rates so the wealthy invest and hire. A Fair Economy analysis found little statistical correlation between top tax rates and GDP, wages or median wealth, though the hosts note hoarding and disputes over results.

segments.title: Obama, quantitative easing and trickle-down monetary policy
segments.summary: The hosts argue Obama's policies are not the opposite of Reagan's, describing quantitative easing as trickle-down monetary policy that mainly helps wealthy Americans.

segments.title: Estate tax proposal
segments.summary: Chuck proposes low income tax rates for the wealthy paired with a heavy estate tax at death to raise revenue and limit dynasties. Josh objects that the government should not decide inheritance and that taxes on wealth still count as tax policy.

segments.title: Closing remarks and listener mail
segments.summary: The hosts wrap up the trickle-down discussion and point to a website article. Then they read listener mail from Caleb in Indiana, who is waiting on dental school applications, and sign off with contact info.
